newsitem.title: CANADA: Foreign buyout no answer for CAI - minister.
newsitem.headline: Foreign buyout no answer for CAI - minister.

text.p: Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson said on Friday that foreign ownership was not an acceptable option for bailing out cash strapped Canadian Airlines International Ltd.

"Foreign ownership is not a solution at all," Anderson told reporters after a parliamentary session. "If there were proposals containing foreign ownership it might jeopardize all our overseas bilateral arrangements with other countries."

There had been widespread speculation that the cash crisis at Canada's second biggest airline might be solved by allowing AMR Corp., the Forth Worth, Texas-based company that controls American Airlines, to increase its share in Canadian.
AMR has a 33-percent ownership interest and 25-percent voting interest in Canadian Airlines International.
Earlier this month Anderson said the government would consider any proposal from AMR, but on Friday he ruled that option out. AMR has not revealed any intention to raise its stake in Canadian.
Anderson said that allowing AMR to buy any more shares in Canadian would give it "effective control" of the airline, thereby jeopardizing Canadian's international service agreements.
Anderson also reiterated his position that government intervention was not the solution to the airline's cash troubles.

"This problem cannot be solved by government intervention. It must be solved by turning that airline into a profitable entity, in the black, as opposed to a non-profitable airline which has lost C$1.3 billion over the last 10 years."
Despite the the dire situation, Canadian officials were optimistic they could work out a restructuring agreement before the November 30 "do-or-die" deadline.

A major breakthrough was achieved on Thursday when the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, the largest of six unions that represent the airline's 16,400 employees, agreed to a 10 per cent pay cut for all of its members that make more than C$30,000.
